patterns: is github the same as git
entries.answer: GitHub is a place to host git repositories and collaborate around them, and it is not the same thing as git itself. The useful parts beyond storage are pull requests, which let a change be reviewed before it lands, and issues, where work gets discussed. Being hosted on GitHub does not make something open source, and the licence file is what decides that.

patterns: how does a pull request work
why is my merge button disabled
entries.answer: A pull request is a proposal to merge one branch into another, and it is the centre of how work gets reviewed on GitHub rather than being merely a way to send code. Opening one lets anyone with access see the exact lines that changed, comment on them, and approve or request changes, so the conversation happens on the code itself rather than in a message. The person who opens it is the author, the person who merges is the maintainer, and the two are often different people, which is the whole point of the arrangement. The checks that matter are the status checks the project has configured, since a build or a test run that fails blocks the merge, and reviewing is a separate requirement from a passing build. A common beginner question is why a merge button is greyed out, and the answer is usually one of these: failing checks, an approval that has not happened yet, or a conflict where the same lines changed on both sides.

patterns: what is a fork on github
what is the difference between fork and clone
how do i contribute to a project
entries.answer: A fork is your own copy of somebody else's repository on the same site, and it is the mechanism that lets someone contribute to a project they do not have write access to. You fork, make your change on your fork, and then open a pull request from your fork to the original, which is why the contribution path works without anyone having to add you as a collaborator. The alternative is for the maintainer to grant access directly, and the reason forks are preferred is scale: a popular project cannot grant access to every person who wants to try a small fix. A fork is also useful for experimenting without touching the original, and a common beginner mistake is to make the change on the original repository instead of on the fork, which then produces a pull request that a maintainer has to ask you to move. A fork falls behind the original over time, so it is pulled down before starting new work if it was created a while ago.
